projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with WIlliam Nehez was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran William S. Nehez. Mr. Nehez served in the U.S. Army in Company A of the 3908th Signal Service Battalion. Bill's highest rank was T5 and he served in the European theater. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Nehez' home in Garfield Heights, Ohio on May 1st, 2003. Bill was 83 at the time of this recording. When did you join the service?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I -- I joined the service and I got kicked out of the service. Because after I had gone through all the examination -- let's say, for instance, a dent -- a dental doctor's examined me, he says, "You can't make it, you have to have a couple cavities taken care of." I says, "Well, you got dentists in the army, don't you?" So he passed me through. Another doctor would say, "I can't pass you; you're supposed to weigh 117 and you only weigh 114." And I looked up at him and I says, "Well, if you were living in depression days and didn't get three meals a day, I think the Army, if they fed me, would pick up that three pounds in a hurry," so he passed me through. And then the doctor, cardiologist, put a stethoscope on my heart and he said, "Can't pass you; you got a heart murmur." I said, "Doctor, if you were sitting" -- it was in the Bradley Building -- "naked, for the last couple hours, in this cold, you'd have a heart murmur, too." So he said, "Go sit over there." And then without telling me he slapped a stethoscope on my heart. He says, "You're okay now." That's how I got in. But, as I say, I originally was kicked out, and then I volunteered for the draft, and went in for the second examination, so they stuck a bunch of needles in me. And I said, "Well, what about this needle I got that says you should have another shot of this in six months and here it's only two months?" Pooh-pooh, forget it. That's the difference.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were actually inducted in early 1941, then?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yes, very much so. Although I had a draft number, it wasn't used. And it kind of humorous to me that the draft number, 152, was similar to my bicycle messenger number, 152.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So where did you train, then?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Well, Pompul (ph) -- that's a friend of mine in the -- in the same good old Hungarian neighborhood -- said, "Tell them that you repair cameras." He says, "This way, it'll keep you out of the infantry." So I told them I repaired cameras, and I wound up in Camp Shelby, Mississippi, with the 112th Engineers, which, of course, also, had almost thirty of the guys from my old Hungarian neighborhood in, so it was a friendly gathering. And then---

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So were you with a -- a signal corps company, then, or were---

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: No, that was the 112th Engineer Combat Battalion --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: -- which, by the way, has a very long and extensive military heritage, going way back in the days of the Bull Run and all that kind of stuff, and of course winding up with the invasion of Europe, Normandy. And then of course nine months training in the United States in Camp Shelby. Then, fortunately, I was on furlough, so when I came back, I found out Companies A, B, C, had been shipped down to the South Pacific, and meantime, Companies D, E and F were slated to go to Europe. But they didn't know what to do with us, at the headquarters in service, so they said, "Send 'em to Europe."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you on December 7th, 1941, when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I was ungodly -- oh, sure, I was down at service at that time, but not overseas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I was in Camp Shelby.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Still Camp Shelby.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your reaction on that day when you heard the news that the war had started?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Well, actually, when the war started with Germany, I didn't feel too bad about it because if war was war, Germany was, I thought, full of human beings, but as scared -- scared of the Japanese, because they were like little wiry rats that could run all around, and I was thankful I didn't get sent to the Pacific because I was on furlough. And then of course I was shipped to Indiantown Gap, P.A., with the three companies, and I, as member of the headquarters service, had landed in Ireland, biv -- bivouacing at Moneymore.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was that crossing like? When did you cross, do you remember? When you made the Atlantic crossing?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: The crossing?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that in early '42 or when was it?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah, it was -- it was lousy. We were on the LS -- LSTs, and as it dipped and doved and rose in the waves, and reeled side to side, I humorously remember a mess kit coming by and said, "Who's lunch is this?" And that was the other thing, and the food was actually pretty doggone good but the gag was you -- you had six meals a day, three going down and three coming up. So then of course we landed in, I believe, the Firth of Clyde, and then went to Belfast. And from Belfast we were trucked to Moneymore, where we spent the next nine months. But I still remember that in Belfast, what would come off the boats first but our piddly little jeeps, and the Irish people looked at us. And I remember north Irish people looked at a Irish we save us newsroom, they looked at it and said -- you could see in their expressions, "They're going to fight a war with these toys?" And then came the bigger equipment, bigger equipment, and their jaws dropped in amazement. But we got to, oh, our area that we were going to stay in. Of course we stayed in a -- a big barn shed or something, and I remember one of my first photographs. I took two of the G.I.s that just were so exhausted they fell asleep, one on curved corrugated tins and another one on some bales. And I took a 15-second exposure, with a fast film we had on that day which was Super Pan, Press Type B, and they didn't move a muscle, and I still have that photograph.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were a photographer from the beginning, then, as soon as you got---

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Essentially -- essentially, I would say, no, I wasn't -- I was a photographer and I was sending material in to The Cleveland News.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: But the photographer in the 112th Engineers, by name of Adorshun (ph) -- he is dead now and buried out here locally -- he was moved up to headquarters, 37th Division. And I can't -- I can tell you the patch was the white circle with a red center but I can't tell you what the G.I.s called it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You can for the Library of Congress.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Well, for the Library, the patch was called The Flaming Asshole. And so I wore that patch until -- and DaVyzeez (ph), the 112th Engineer, took on another -- either engineer or infantry unit. I believe it had bade (ph) engineers, who had a camera, and then their unit was folded and they were added to ours. Well, that unit's cameraman was a brown-noser, and so when the officers of this new unit, assigned to ours, wanted me to photograph their girls and their dances and their parties, I said no, that it was a misuse of American equipment. So their answer was to put me on the shit details, latrine -- latrine duty, mess hall and all that kind of stuff. And so when the 112th Engineers had a football game, the first football game I ever played, in the United Kingdom, that the king and queen was to attend, I was sent down, as the engineer photographer, to photograph it. Now this, I said, was all right. In my mind, it was showing the joining of the two nations, England, Great Britain, United Kingdom and -- and, of course, United States. So I -- I photographed a game, and while I was photographing the game I noticed a lieutenant, a tall, slender, walking toward me. So I smartly came to a salute and he introduced himself. He said, I am Lieutenant Perham (ph), (yawning) from London, in a signal corps. He says, "I -- I notice you seem to know what you're doing with the camera." Well, just a quick flashback: United States Camera -- and were trained in Astoria, New York, and they got sergeant stripes, but when they came over, to England, they didn't know how to use a camera. So the lieutenant queried about me. I said, "Yes, I was working for the Cleveland News" -- a big fib at that time -- "as a cameraman, and I pretty well know what makes this thing tick." He says, "How would you like to come into London to work for the signal corps?" I said, "No problem. When do I move?" So, after the game, a couple weeks later, I was very -- rather surprised to find out that I had orders that I was -- pack up my gear and report down to London. Well, I remember getting down to London all right. Went there, smartly saluted the officer that I reported to, and he says, "Well, I think we can put you in a darkroom making prints." And I told him straight to his face, "I came down here as a cameraman. If you don't want me as a cameraman, ship me back." And just then, fortunately, Lieutenant Perlman (ph) walked by, and he says, "This is my boy, I'll take care of him." So next thing I knew I was a cameraman.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So before you went into the army you had a part-time job as a photographer, with The Cleveland News?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yes, I drove -- I was working one day out of the week, no pay, but I was also giving in stories and photographs.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is there someone calling you? (Interview interrupted by unidentified speaker). ____+

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So approximately when did you get to Northern Ireland? Would that be sometime in 1942?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I would say 1942. We'd -- we'd have to look in the album.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But some -- I don't need the exact dates.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah, I would say about 1942 I was a cameraman. And before I left the 112th, it wasn't that I was angry but I was rather --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Bye-bye.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: -- rather theatrical. And I said, well, I'm going to just tack on my private first class stripes and I'm going to give Captain Green (ph) these stripes when I move out. So I did that. That was a stupid thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's when you left the 112th?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yes, I left the 112th. I was then on the -- it was for eight 10th Signal Corps Headquarters, then it became the 3908.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And after I got down there I was a Pfc., I was sent out on Detachment F, which was in Cheltenham, and which, by the way, was also the unit that Lieutenant Perlma (ph) was with. A couple months later, Lieutenant Perham (ph) came up to me and -- at this time, saluting was forgot -- forgotten. He said, "Bill" -- he said, "I tried like hell to jump you three -- three grades to a sergeant but I could only jump you to corporal technician." So I became a corporal technician and remained a corporal technician for the rest of my service years, of about four to go, because these guys that were training Astoria, New York came overseas with sergeant stripes and they filled up our table of organization so there was no place for me to move up. And that was that part of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was life like in Great Britain during those days?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I thought it was pretty neat and clean. We were in London and also I was in Cheltenham. And the only war that I saw, at that time, was when Germany made the V-1s. Now the V-1s, they were nice. They came over like a little plane buzz, buzzing along. And by a timer in them, they cut off the timer, then they would dive and blow up. Well, that was bad enough, added being that if you heard it putt-putting, putting, you tried to get its location, and if it didn't hit, in three seconds, you had two seconds to dive for cover. But then the Germans got smart. They -- they got a V-1, when the Germans got control, and the timer, instead of shutting off the engine, would first kick in the rudder and the damn thing would circle over and over and over your head, you didn't know which way it was going to land. But I saw a couple of them actually come down, and they didn't look frightening but naturally, if they hit a building, hopefully, people would be out of it, in the air raid shelters. If they had a playground or like that, kids wouldn't be out, school would be out, and so I saw them. And then -- we're still in Ireland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Oh, excuse me. No, we've gotten to London by now because I'm talking about the London buzz bombs. I don't know of any that actually hit North Ireland, although the aircraft did. But in England, in London, I was assigned to quickly get in a jeep with another cameraman and, if people asked, just say "a gas main blew up." Well, actually, the gas main was the first V-2, which was truly a rocket, and it would come up and then come down, and in a proximity fuse would blow up in the air, shattering shrapnel and stuff in all directions, instead of just hitting the ground and blowing upward, negating much of the damage it could do. But a laughable story about that, and which I regretted I didn't get later, was a WAAC who was in a billet in London. And so one of these blooming things blew up outside of her window, and shattered the glass. It sliced her rear end open. She got a purple heart for that. And me, I almost got killed three times and I never got a purple heart. So that mean -- meant nothing but it meant a hell of a lot when you were up for points for discharge. Okay, son. Anything else?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you go through any air raids, traditional air raids, when you were over there in Great Britain?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yes, I was in an -- an air raid. In fact, the album I showed you the free sketch that I drew---

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, go ahead and tell me that.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I remember being down in a building, and I ran up the stairs, when I heard the air raid sirens, and I was stopped by one of their home guards wearing a helmet. He says, "You can't come out here." I had my camera. I says, "Yes, I can." I showed him my identification, and I said, "I'll stay close to the buildings, but I want to get to where that bomb hit." And he says, "Okay, but you know you're on your own risk." So I looked up and there I caught in the -- in those -- events flashlights. I forget what they call them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Search lights? Search lights?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Search lights. Was a German plane. And it twists and then it dodged. It looked like a shiny nickel. But these search -- search lights followed him until either he managed to get away or I don't know what. But then also another bomb hit, and I could see the flash silhouetting the buildings and then a wave of black smoke poured over the buildings and then engulfed me. And so then when it passed me by I went toward the -- the flash zone and, here, a building completely gone, and its structure was shining white, like skeletons. And that was my experience in the first raid. Of course, naturally, you -- you're never going to get killed, you got God up there protecting you, so you stick your neck into foolish places and you come out alive. And then they -- next -- next thing I'd like to state is when the V-2 hit, the first V-2. And when I went there, the jeep driver and the camera and I, we were turned back by home guard. So, the jeep driver just went around the corner, found an alley, and he went down there, there was another home guard at that end of the alley. And he said, "Who let you in?" We showed the guy the credentials up there and he let us in. So we went in there and in no time at all found the debris that they had already collected from V-1. Portions of gears and metal and all that kind of jazz, and I photographed that stuff. And then a lady was being interviewed, by one of the home guard. I went over and listened in. She -- she said, "There's four of us playing cards, and all of a sudden the building was gone and I was left at the table by myself." So that meant three were killed. And that's it -- you know, as far as the war in London. The V -- V-1s, the jerrors (ph) kept turning in circles, V-1, and then the V-2. That's basically the only war that I saw in London.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were your assignments as a photographer when you were in London? Did you just go out and get whatever you could get or did you have specific---

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Well, from my newspaper sense, I would photograph things which I thought were interesting, but most of them were assignments. Traditionally awards, this and that unit's moving, parades and all that. God, the British were crazy about parades.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And so I would photograph those.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And then, doing my best to stay off of K.P. and latrine duty.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get along with -- go ahead. You had something else?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah, I got along with the---

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The British people?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Oh, yeah, very much so. And in fact, now, this is so many years after war, it always comes in my mind, that especially the grit -- the British girls, they would want to marry Americans, so that they can get a free ride back to the States. But I -- I wasn't of the marriaging -- marriageable mood and as -- if you notice, some of the photographs in the album, there were some very beautiful girls that I had -- I was very fortunate to meet.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And I would like to state at this time that I'm not only fortunate in that I met them but fortunate that they were ladies, notwithstanding the other junk that these G.I.s would pick up. So that's that so far.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So tell me about the -- the preparations for D-day then, the invasion of -- of the Normandy (ph).

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Well, I had been based in Cheltenham for almost a couple years, when the invasion came around. Of course, nobody knew it was the invasion. They'd been practicing for months and years on the English Channel, loading and unloading and all that kind of jazz. But we knew something was afoot when out of all the cameramen, and reporters in the signal corps, they chose ten teams; one was a G.I. reporter, and, in my case, his name was McDonald (ph), Sergeant Erwin McDonald, and the other one was a movie man. In my case, it was Fred Safeeda (ph). And then I, as a still photographer. And we were sent down to an area, a new zone area, roughly ten miles wide, along the southern coast of England, and you didn't get in that area unless you had the proper credentials. So I went into the area and I -- again, I did a stupid thing. I was doing some photography and I already passed through the thing, and I told this officer -- I should say the word "told." I didn't ask him. I told this officer, "You know, here I've been taking photographs of this area," I said, "How the hell you don't -- don't you know that I'm a spy?" He says, "Well, if I thought you were a spy, I'd" sell -- "tell you to start running and you'd get shot in the back." That's how it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Ten miles, real controlled. Nobody would get -- get in unless they had a reason to be there. So, after we did some of the traditional photography, wound up at Extra (ph) Airfield, which is rather south, even west of Portsmouth, England, and we were assigned planes because we were asked, the three of us, if we would like to go on a milk run. Well, who's going to get killed? So we went on a milk run. And then about thirty seconds before takeoff time Captain White, of the 5th -- 1st Observation -- this is what I remember -- came over and said, "You know, we have to balance the weights on these planes, so you're going to change your position, your plane, with Sergeant Erwin McDonald, to get the weights close together." Well, Erwin McDonald couldn't have been ten pounds lighter than I --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: -- but we changed, and we made the milk run. And then as we made the milk run and turned around I looked out the cargo door, the C-47 with the invasion stripes, and the place where Sergeant Erwin -- Erwin McDonald's plane was to be was not there. So I kept looking. Now I know -- they didn't show up. So then when we landed, we went to the interrogation hut. They were passing out one shot of whiskey to every -- everybody that had been on that particular flight. And they offered me the whiskey and I says, "No thanks, I don't drink." So then, after the interrogation, one of the men -- I can't remember if -- remember if it was an officer or not -- oh, now -- now I recall. He was a pilot of the C-47 that McDonald was in. And he was very sorrowful. He said, "You know, we got hit. And my" pote (ph) -- "co-pilot died. But I opened the cabin door and looked back, and out of the seven people aboard the plane," he says, "four of them were stacked against the pack -- parachute packs that didn't get shoved out in time." And he says, "We were able to make it, to England." But one of the other pilots told them that they were over the channel when all of a sudden the top of their plane split open like a can opener. So he turned around and went back to England and, fortunately, he was able to land.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And I didn't know if he landed on the fields, the airfield, or just on the fields, but he made it back over the cliffs of Dover and landed. And later on -- I wish I had that letter they sent me -- they said that the only way that plane had been hit was by friendly fire. They're all our ships in the channel. Somehow, a shell had been short-loaded and it went up and it came down. Whole expanse of the sky and these two things met. So a Sergeant Erwin McDonald, whose story is in there, in the album, died. And whether his parents, who live down in St. Petersburg, Florida, got his body back I don't know, because although I went to vacation several times, to St. Petersburg, I never looked them up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that happened on D-day?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: D plus one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: D plus one?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: It was a milk run. Supply with parawacs (ph) and parapacks (ph). Parapacks were shoved out, out of the cargo door, and had their parachute hooked up to the cable. Parawacs were carried in like the bomb racks, underneath -- underneath the plane's wings and their parachute was triggered.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you went along to photograph that mission?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I photographed that mission. In fact, I looked down and chuckled when I saw the cows running around a field. And then I saw a flash of fire, and said, "Look that guy, that stupid German trying to hit that plane." Well, while we were in the air, a shaft of light shot across in front of the jump sergeant who was pushing out the parawacs, or parapacks, and he said, "Christ, that's a bullet. Let's get out of here." So we turned around and went back to England. When we got out of the plane, he counted four bullet holes. Years later, he thought to me, hell, I'm sticking with my camera, my head and my shoulders, and my leg wrapped around the strut of the seat, of the C-47. That guy wasn't shooting at the plane, he was shooting me. So that's -- that was it. I got out alive.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now there's a -- since we don't -- I could have a copy of the picture but there's a famous picture. Now where did that appear, in the -- the Life picture that you have of the airborne guys, of the C-47s?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah, that was on the night of D-day, twilight was falling, and to get this shot, there's two paths I'd crossed and there's a parked jeep. I jumped on top of the jeep.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And I said, "God, I have no light." I couldn't use a flashbulb because a flashbulb is only good for about fifteen feet, then it's no good. Everything in the background will be black. So I was one of the few cameraman that -- who was trained by a newspaper, and to hell with high -- light meters. I had two in my head; my eyes. So I -- I guessed a shutter speed on the focal plane shutter, the speed graphic, at a fifteenth of a second, the lowest possible speed a human being could hold steady, and I guessed 4.5, which was the largest lens opening, that lens in -- let light through the lens into the camera, and I stood up there and I braced my feet and I braced myself -- something I can't do today at 85 -- and, fortunately, a troop of soldiers went by and the last one, slung over his shoulder, had a bazooka. So I triggered a shot. And when I got back to Cheltenham, I found out that it was just short of a perfect negative but that it could be printed and that was a -- picked as one of the best hundred photos of World War II, by Life Magazine, and then ap -- appeared, also, in Life's Pictorial History of World War II. And that was one of the amazing things that I thought that could happen. Here I am, I -- really on the outside of the war looking in, halfway between a -- a correspondent of today's war and the war that we knew then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When was that Life pictorial published, of the -- do you remember when that was, the book?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I'd have -- I'd have to grab it out of the book --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Approximately --

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: -- yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- ten years ago, something like that or more?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Oh, geez, I'd say about ten years ago easy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Sometime maybe the fiftieth anniversary --

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- of the war?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: That's right, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And so -- you know since -- people listening to this tape might be able -- I'm sure they'll be able to find copy of that picture.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah, I think it's on page forty-nine, runs across almost two pages of the top.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It's a panoramic shot, with lots of C-47s.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Panoramic shot, and then you could see the C-47s and other aircraft in the background. You can see the G.I. with the platoon --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: -- with the bazooka shot over his -- laying over his shoulder --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: -- and that would identify it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: There's a group of paratroopers, one marching kind of down the road---

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I -- I don't know that they didn't carry equipment, so they must have been paratroopers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, that's -- I guess we don't know that for sure. This will describe it, in case people---

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: That's the surprising thing, because in the engineers, I had that steel pop, which you tried on which you realize is rather heavy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And I had the ground rifle, and I had the M-14, and I was protected. When I went into the signal corps, they took away my helmet, they took away my firearms, they didn't even even give me a side arm, and I was supposed to go into enemy country just with a camera. In fact, I have a book that I just bought, and it's very -- rather interesting. Better -- it has names of cameramen I knew. It is called Armed, With Cameras. It's a story about the signal corps, overseas in Europe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And it's very interesting because when I wrote in to Washington, about getting information about the 3908 and eight tenth, they had so little amount on it that it -- it's as if it hadn't even existed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you go over to France?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I went over to France actually on D plus four.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I went over on an LST, and it was a nur -- nursing assignment -- makes you laugh -- to photograph the nurses in their brand new uniforms.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And then it also came back that story that the Germans were wondering what secret weapon we had because there's a bunch of tubes sticking out of the ground pointing toward -- toward Germany, and the Germans were scared as to what that new secret weapon was. They were urinals, for the guards. All they did was take out their whatsiz (ph) and peed on the pipe. The nurses, of course, had -- not tents, they had field wraps, that screened them from the G.I.s.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And then this is where I also -- I don't -- I think I photographed and yet I don't think I photographed it. But I kept the story, the letter she wrote, day before she was killed, and it's in the album there. Her name was Lieutenant Francis Langer (ph). She was the first American killed -- American nurse killed, and a story was that on that -- the Germans strafed the hospital, although it was clearly marked, and she died in the hands of another nurse holding her intestines, because they'd been shot out from her. So that's when you feel that war is coming close to you. And then when you went overseas -- I mean not overseas, but over in the Germany, we were giving these children the clickers, that being you clicked once, and if you got an answer, two clicks back, that meant that was friend there. But if one click came back, hey, that guy's an enemy, and you steered clear of the area, or you laid low, until you can get a shot at him. And this was needed, in England, and other foreign lands because their idea of fences, there were hedgerows, and you could lay on one side and you can hear them talk German on the other side. But if you had no thing, then you advance and you would click this clicker, which sounded like a -- what the hell do you call it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I know, a cricket, or whatever they call them.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah, a cricket. They sounded like crickets.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Like they always talked about using them when the --

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- Airborne went in on D-day, they would use those to identify each other.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah. So you clicked once, as you were friend.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And the response is twice.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And if you got two click -- clicks back, that your -- you had a friend, you were fine, but if only one click back -- came back, you had to be very, very cautious.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where did you land in France, when you landed France?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: In France?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: One of the -- which one of the beaches?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: No, I -- let me mull this over in my -- my mind. The 112th Engineers that I had left -- and they had suffered fifty percent casualties -- that doesn't mean dead, that means fifty percent either dead or wounded.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And -- they landed on Omaha Beach and presumably they were the ones that breached that Atlantic wall that Germany had come up, which, of course, is in the film of The Dirty Dozen.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: But -- let me see. I know I went across on boat, that's right. I went on -- across on boat about D plus four --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: -- past sunken ships and other stuff, and then I embarked on a runabout or something to take me to the shore.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And then they was by thumbs and credentials, where my move would be.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Well, naturally, that was just a small move inside Omaha Beach, which then---

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you did land on Omaha Beach.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Oh, yes, I landed on Omaha Beach.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So was it still a mess there---

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: By that time, the firing was sort of over.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Because the Americans had moved in fairly quick, and the Rangers, which were supposed to nullify, or negate some guns, which could sweep to right and left, getting both beaches plus the---

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: God, is that the English Channel? Oh, well.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Well, anyway, when the Rangers got there and rappelled up that so -- so-called cliff, it was a hundred feet high, frank -- frankly, I don't think it was thirty feet high but whatever it was, it was high.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And when they got to the top they found out that the Germans had moved the guns back, about two to four miles.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And naturally the guns were knocked out, by the ships. So that -- that's as far as I can recall going on that trip.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I was concentrating wounding (ph) -- mainly on the beach and then getting back where -- aboard the LST took us back. One of the medical officers said, "Hey, come on over here," and he took me over to a German soldier. You -- you could tell they were German soldiers, not because the uniform, because they were sitting on the metal planking of the LST and he says -- in German, I guess, he told this guy, "Raise your arm," and the guy raised his arm, and a shot of light went right through his arm. And he says, "Look at this guy, how lucky he is." A bullet got him in the armpit, went through his shoulder muscles, bone and everything, didn't hit anything, came out through the top. So, as the bullet went through, it cauterized the wound, and now all we're going to tell him is, "In winter, if it feels cold, stuff cotton in it." So that was one thing. But the American soldiers that were wounded, oh, they were -- they weren't lucky in a sense but they were lucky that they were on hammocks that had been attached to the inside of the -- of the boats, and so they were able to get a comfortable resting period. And that was where I first really saw the LST in action. The LSTs were made here in Cleveland, at least one of the services, by the White Motor Company on about 73rd and St. Clair. But those buggers would circle around and hit the beach. They'd be loaded with injured and all that kind of stuff. Circle around and come to the ramp, up the ramp, unload the injuries and all, all that stuff again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. You're talking about---

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Then go back in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you're talking about a -- a duck (ph), right?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: A duck.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: A D.U.K.W.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A D.U.K.W.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: But it was commonly referred to as a duck.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, the amphibian land---

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Well, that they would waddle in the water.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And they could go up on land?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah, they could go on land.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Up on the ship, too, as you say.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And then the ship was probably the LST, naturally which had a water ramp, come down and they'd have to get to so much depth in the shore from the ramp to hit ground and let these ducks come around insert -- oh, excuse me, the ducks in water could circle around to the ramp and come up the ramp.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: If the duck was going to let off troops, it would come up until it hit ground, then drop the ramp for the ground troops to get off.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum? Now did you go back and forth between France and England?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I made, actually, three trips.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: The second trip was the Red Ball Express.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah. Well, the Red Ball Express -- and I hope I can say this in a way that it doesn't harm or -- harm or make somebody feel bad. But the Red Ball Express, its trucks were all banned (ph) by whom we refer to now as African-Americans. The African-Americans were drivers of these trucks. And of course these trucks went with covered-over lights and then the blue parking lights were very faint. Some of them were or were not covered, depending on the area. But the convoy was under the control -- and laugh if you want -- of a white officer. Well, I found -- followed this American (ph) convoy, for the -- from the docks of Portsmouth. END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE. I and Alan Sisner (ph), the cameraman, movie cameraman, army, chose to follow not bullets and bombs but to follow a gas valve, of a field stove, fourteen hundred yards to the Germans. They were -- had two field stoves put away with one down, it meant the men could only count for one war meal a day. And we followed this bugger valve, from the truck to -- to the docks, to the ships, to the docks, to the trucks, all the way up to Butgenbach, Germany, which, by the way, was almost ankle deep in mud. But they would -- the hundred -- excuse me, I can't think of the -- it's Howitzer unit, 135 millimeters, somewhere, was not in the town but outside of the town, and the Germans were in a town fourteen hundred yards away. So I thought a fitting shot would be to have one shell, sent off toward Germany. So this poor kid, this G.I., had nothing more than a field jacket, and here it was zero degrees, and I had at least an army coat. And I was going to give it to him but I said, "What's going to keep me warm?" So, anyway, I talked it over with the guy. He says, "Oh, he says, "I -- they give me fifteen shells a night." He says, "I can fire them all at once or one at a time, just to keep the damn Germans awake." So I says, "Okay, I'll -- I'll set up my camera. You fire me one." So I signaled, he fired. But I didn't know enough about photography. I should have set the camera up, and photographed the Howitzer, 155 milliliter (sic) Howitzer, just in the fading daylight, and then with the camera on tripod, not moving, then shoot the shell being fired. Then I would have a double image which would show a front line Howitzer fronting. This way I got practically nothing. But anyway, I headed back, to London, via route -- by the convoy. And all I had was a travel orders. We holed up at a -- a French chalet. I slept on a kitchen table. The sergeant, I don't know where he slept. We put all our camera equipment, movie and still, in the back end of the convoy, in the truck. So what do we do? We wake up in the morning, and the roosters are crowing. No convoy. Camera equipment? Gone. The sergeant remembered some of the numbers. So, can you imagine? In the middle of the war, only carrying a piece of mimeograph travel orders, we hitchhike back to Paris. On the way, hitchhiking, we passed a very French-looking man and his cute little daughter. And in our broken French -- that time we signed, a hand signals -- signaled, he was going our way. Oh, come on aboard. So he came on aboard. We -- we didn't speak French, neither of them spoke American or English. And behind the tarp on the truck was sea rations, so we stole some of them and gave it to them. Well, we -- we got about halfway to their destination when an M.P. stopped our truck and says -- they just say they live down there but we can't speak French and they can't speak English. So the M.P. talked to them in French, and he told them to get off the jeep, jeep and the convoy. And -- and I'm sorry to see them go, they were such -- such nice people and I -- I hope they made it all right. But we got back, to London, Paris, and I told the sergeant, "Well, you go bivouac somewhere, and I'll find out if I can find a transportation officer and find the equipment." He says, "Okay." I didn't see him for four days. And he had his fun at Paris, because when I got it back to Paris -- and I had found the equipment -- he said, "Let's go." "Well, what happened in Paris, I walked into the transportation officer's office, on the Champs Elysees, clicked my whole -- heels and smart -- smartly saluted, looked like a dog-eareded (sic) G.I., because of growth of beard and all that, and when he looked up, he says, "Bill, what the hell are you doing here?" Can you imagine? Here's a guy, way in Paris, used to date my daughter back in Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Your sister.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah. So, the outcome was, he gave me a jeep and a driver and he says, "Don't come back till you get the equipment." It took four days to find the equipment. I got back and then he took me to his apartment, and I slept there overnight. He took me the next day to get me English oxford shoes instead of the clodhoppers I was wearing. And, boy, was I tickled pink. And so I said good-bye to him and then caught the LST for Eng -- England. By the way, some of you that don't recall an LST, they are very similar to namesakes of the English boats that ply the channel now and drop a ramp, and unload cars, cows, human beings, whatever. And that recently hit, about a year ago, in one in which one of the crewmen forgot to close a front damp -- ramp, and when it moved over from the dock, it keeled over and capsized, everything under the decks was gone. I don't recall how many people were drowned or killed. But that is what an LST really is. It's what the English are now using -- and maybe other countries -- for landing near docks, and discarging (ph) cargo.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now following the Red Ball Express, you said that was your second trip to France?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your third trip?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Third trip? Boy, I got to remember that one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: If you can.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I all -- already got -- talked about D plus one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And then the Red Ball trip. Express trip. God, you know, I can't pick it out of my mind?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's all right.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And I can't pick it out of my mind, even the albums. But I -- I will say -- say this, that the average G.I., even today, goes over, he says, "I'm not going to get killed." Well, how -- how do--- Oh, yes. It was part of the Ever All (ph) Express. I was going along, Sisna (ph) and I were standing up in the back of this pickup truck, and we noticed on two sides of the roadway, in the ditches, the G.I.s were hunched down. And I laughed to myself, you know, and I thought, wow. Then, I says, "Look at those G.I.s playing soldier." And then just then, a whack. And a driver hit the brakes, we slammed up against the back of the cab and then we were over the side, and down with the G.I.s before we said, "Hell, our cameras are still in the truck." And the outfit was, they were being pinned down by a sniper. And the word had passed up on the line to hit the ditch. Well, they couldn't tell the truck driver that, who had come along unexpected. And we were in the ditch maybe out fifteen minutes, and then a G.I. or an officer came to line -- down line and he says, "Sir, don't worry about the sniper, we took care of him." And so we got up and continued on with the pickup truck to our destination, which is Butgenbach, Germany. Of course, we didn't know it. But I can't -- I can't for the life of me remember the -- the third -- third thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's all right. Maybe it will come to you. Yeah, you photographed Bob Hope. Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Oh, Bob Hope was one of the real biggies of the U.S.O. And his one -- one-liners were -- were terrific. And I thought I'd -- I could say hello to him, because I was a camera, I moved around freely. But Martha Raye what -- was his sidekick, and she had that great laughable kick of putting one arm under the arm -- armpit and flapping it up and down and look -- sound like a series of farts. But, other than that, I thought Bob Hope was pretty good. But, when I wanted a -- and I did tell him, that he was in a company of the 112th Engineers, Cleveland, Ohio, I don't think it phased him. I thought he'd go down and say -- holler to the guys, but no, he just went through his routine and that was it. But he was -- he was a nice guy. Later on, after the war, my -- after the war, I dated a -- a lovely girl whose mother owned a restaurant, right behind The Cleveland News, and Bob Hope was in town, and I was assigned to cover him. So I told her exactly this: I made up a print of Bob Hope overseas, and he came down, in -- in between a row of ropes, keep other people away, and I said, "I'm going to show this to Bob Hope, and he's going to stop. And you get ready, to be next to him, and I'll take the photograph."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And Bob Hope came down and I just stood there with my camera. I was inside the ropes because of being a newspaper photographer. And I waited, photos, so he took one look and he came over, took it out of my hands, and he says, "Oh, boy," words to the effect, where'd you get this? And then the girl, on my signal, she ducked under -- underneath the ropes. I said, "Would you mind being photographed with my girl friend?" He said -- he said words, no, or whatever, and I still have that photograph.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And she was tickled pink.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And he was tickled pink to get a -- a photograph which he knew was him overseas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: And I -- I kind of liked him but he was -- he was a busy guy. But I'm kind of surprised that he didn't think of remembering Cleveland, Ohio and 112th Engineers, that he was like a brother to them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: So that was a -- oh, a short little thing. You know, he'd had a white knight -- one-night stand and -- and then after the show got in his tent. In the morning he was driven by his driver where he was at. There was another guy on his show, I couldn't photograph and he pleaded with me to get a photograph -- photograph of him doing his act. His act could have been something but it was a nothing camera wise, because what he would do is get three or four people from the audience, and they would carry a -- a conversation in front of him, and then he would repeat that conversation as it came out of their mouths.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Well, that was great, but I couldn't show that on camera.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: So he was all right. And of course a song bird, Frances Langford, was with him, and she was nice.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You talked to her?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I can't remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not really---

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I mean, it -- you could -- you could talk to a lot of these people, just as in forty years of newspaper work I talked to a lot of people, some famous, some not, I don't remember them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you -- did you take any other famous people, photographs of famous people during the war, recognizable people? You took a picture of Churchill, I know.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah, Churchhill, and then a couple of the army, navy, marine and you -- let's see. Army, navy, marine.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Air force.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Air corps. People that happened to be in front of my camera.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: But, as I say, being a cameraman, you get a lot of beautiful things pass. There's a passing parade and here you are living, sitting down, enjoying your life as best you can. You remember them. They're -- they're in your head, but it's like a bandstand playing up there. But I -- I'll tell you, you may have heard it before, but for a million dollars, I wouldn't have missed the war. For a million dollars, I would have liked to have stayed out of the war, because after the war was over it was scrambling, trying to get back into the world that was there. And living with the story in your head, of a guy that works down in the veterans' building, getting a hundred dollars a month, ever since World War II is over, wearing a Congressional Medal of Honor, which he doesn't deserve. He knows it, I know it, and the reporter from The Cleveland Press knows it. And this poor G.I., a sergeant, showed us the scars in his hand, introduced to his wife and his two children, he could use that hundred dollars a month. But what do I do? Die with that story in my mind?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So this is somebody that -- no names but this is somebody that got a Congressional Medal of Honor that shouldn't have?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Well, he has it, and he has the award certificate of what he did that earned him the Congressional Medal of Honors, but he doesn't know what he did, except what's written on the certificate.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, so, he doesn't remember it; is that what you're saying?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He doesn't remember doing this?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Oh, he remembers, but he doesn't want to dispute the authority of the lieutenant that came next to the shell hole and heard this story. And since that war in Vietnam --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: -- was a bad war --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: -- and the military, and the government was looking for heroes---

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, are you talking about a Medal of Honor --

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah, I'm---

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- medal from Vietnam?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I'm sorry, yeah, I should have -- shouldn't have jumped a gap.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, I -- I thought you were talking about World War II now.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: No. I wish I could---

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You're talking about a Medal of Honor winner from Vietnam.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah. And I wish -- well, you know, when I think of military service, I think my brothers and sisters, and all that, and we engulfed the whole --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: -- military.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about World War II, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah. You mean this other guy? Just a minute. Yeah, his memory comes to mind---

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No -- yeah.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Pardon? What?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you, personally, think about World War II --

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Again, as a cameraman, you would have a lot of vivid memories. I would think one of the vivid humorous memories I have is on the Red Ball Express, when I went in -- into this warehouse area that the trucks were unloading, I met this -- oh, pretty, pretty French girl. Well, I was a G.I., I want to make time with girls. So I ask her, "How do I look a French girl in the eyes and tell her she's beautiful?" She smiled and she says, "Oh, just tell her, 'You are un moche'" (ph). Un moche. Well, it wasn't until I got back that I -- and got the French translation -- and I hope it's correct -- that I was telling her, to this girl, that she was a dog. But that's the thing that I remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Of course I'll remember getting an aerial photograph, of a camp in England. And the only way to get an aerial photograph -- stupidly, I didn't requisition an airplane -- was to climb up a water tower. But the water tower ladder was split and you had to step across almost ten feet of open space. Well, I stepped across and remained on the ladder for the next fifteen rungs to the top of the water. Then I got on the top of the water and then it's a big, floating disc about twenty feet. And I sat down in middle, getting my courage, to sneak over to the edge, and take some photographs, four different directions, aerial photographs, with the camera. And then I crawled back to the center, and then the fog rolled in. And believe me, an English fog is you put your hand in front of a -- your face? You don't see nothing. I sat for maybe an hour and a half, in a center of that damn water tower, until the fog rolled by. And then I figured, how do I get down? It's easy climbing up, but when you climb up you're not supposed to look down. And here was this ten-foot gap of ladders that I had to look down and see. I think my hair started turning right then. But that's -- there's so much.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: I mean, you had a chance to look through those albums. You didn't have the chance to read a lot of this story material. If you did, you'd finally find a lot there that you would have missed, or that you -- you would have missed because I'm talking this mic.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, just for the purposes of the tape, I've gone through three scrapbooks here, and there are a total of twelve hundred and sixty-four items in these scrapbooks.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah, that's including---

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Including pictures, newspaper articles --

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- journal entries and various---

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: You got jerks' petty drawings, everything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So they're really great scrapbooks and I wish the people listening to this tape could see it.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah, well, sometime when you've got a lazy day --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Whatever time is that?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: -- in summer, tell me to bring them out and I'll have my daughter drive me out and---

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, exactly. That would be nice.

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: But I don't consider my (sic) a hero, I just went along with the times. And the fact that I'm sitting here talking to you is just because a good guy upstairs still hasn't told me what he put me here on earth for, and I'm waiting for him to call me. And here I'm eighty-five and he hasn't whispered yet. So that's -- that's what it is.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Very good. Do you think that covers it for now, as much as we can anyway?

sp.speaker: William Nehez
sp.p: Yeah.
